query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of a Si-based dopant into ZrB2 formulations enables spark plasma sintering at lower temperatures (∼1600–1700 °C) and, through in situ formation of a protective secondary phase (e.g., a borosilicate or SiO2 layer), markedly improves oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance compared with both high-temperature (>2300 °C) single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature specimens prepared without the dopant.
generation.material_initial_state: Traditional single-phase ZrB2, typically prepared at temperatures above 2300 °C and lacking added dopants, which shows vulnerability to high-temperature oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion.
generation.intervention: Addition of a Si-based dopant followed by spark plasma sintering at reduced temperatures (1600–1700 °C) under an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Sintering performed at 1600–1700 °C under inert gas; subsequent exposure to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 1200–1400 °C in air) and liquid-metal plating bath environments matching service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an in situ protective secondary phase (likely a borosilicate or silica-based phase) at the grain boundaries that enhances interfacial adhesion and provides a passivating layer against oxidation and corrosion.
generation.mechanism: The Si-based dopant reduces the sintering activation energy, allowing full densification at lower temperatures. Simultaneously, during sintering and/or subsequent thermal exposure, it reacts to form a protective, self-passivating secondary phase that shields the ZrB2 matrix from high-temperature oxidation and corrosive liquid metal environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: The doped ZrB2 will exhibit full densification and structural integrity at sintering temperatures of 1600–1700 °C, along with enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance and reduced liquid plating-metal corrosion when compared to both conventional high-temperature (above 2300 °C) single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature specimens lacking the dopant.
generation.baseline: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared at over 2300 °C and lower-temperature specimens prepared without a Si-based dopant, which suffer from oxidation and corrosion issues.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within the sintering temperature window of 1600–1700 °C and under service conditions reaching up to approximately 1200–1400 °C for oxidation tests, as well as under representative liquid-plating metal corrosion environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration and its distribution must be optimized; potential phase segregation or unexpected secondary phases may form, which could impact mechanical properties. The precise magnitude of the enhancement in oxidation and corrosion resistance is uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 samples: one set doped with a calibrated Si-based additive and a control set without dopant. Use spark plasma sintering at 1650 °C under an inert atmosphere for both sample sets. After sintering, subject the samples to high-temperature oxidation tests at 1200–1400 °C in air and liquid plating-metal corrosion tests under standardized conditions. Perform phase analysis using XRD to check for the formation of the protective secondary phase, and assess densification, hardness, and structural integrity via SEM and mechanical testing.
measurements: Sintering temperature achievement and densification level (using density measurements and microstructural SEM analysis)
Phase composition before and after oxidation (using XRD and TEM to detect the protective secondary phase)
High-temperature oxidation performance (mass gain and scale adherence during oxidation tests)
Liquid-metal corrosion behavior (weight loss, surface morphology, and integrity after corrosion tests)
Mechanical properties (hardness and fracture toughness measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-doped samples do not show lower-temperature densification (i.e., similar or poorer densification compared to controls), or if they do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance and liquid-metal corrosion behavior relative to both the high-temperature single-phase and lower-temperature non-doped samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In addition to the intrinsic benefits induced by the use of this additive, a positive effect was derived by the in situ synthesis of both ceramic constituents during the SHS and SPS stages. This is expected to highly promote the establishment of strong interfaces between the formed phases and, consequently, enhance the performances of resulting material.
